animals.behavior_notes: Chinook Salmon, the largest Pacific salmon, make their fall spawning runs up rivers like the Hoh and Elwha, where they can be seen thrashing through shallow gravel beds to deposit eggs. Their large size and dark spawning coloration make them relatively easy to identify.
animals.viewing_tips: Walk the Hoh River Trail in Olympic National Park in September and scan clear, shallow gravel sections; polarized sunglasses are essential for cutting through surface glare to spot fish below.

animals.name: Sockeye Salmon
parks: Lake Clark National Park and Preserve
animals.behavior_notes: Sockeye Salmon turn brilliant red with green heads during their spawning run, making them one of the most visually striking salmon to observe. They congregate in enormous numbers in streams and lake shallows, creating an unforgettable spectacle.
animals.viewing_tips: The Brooks River and adjacent areas of Lake Clark NP offer outstanding viewing; visit in late July or early August and watch from designated viewing platforms to avoid disturbing fish and bears.

animals.name: Coho Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Coho Salmon enter coastal streams and rivers in fall, often penetrating smaller tributaries that other salmon species ignore, making them viewable in surprisingly accessible locations. They display bright red flanks and hooked jaws as the spawn approaches.
animals.viewing_tips: Scout smaller tributary streams in Olympic National Park after heavy autumn rains raise water levels; coho follow rising water quickly and can appear in streams that looked nearly empty days before.

animals.name: Steelhead Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Steelhead Trout are sea-run rainbow trout that return to freshwater rivers in winter and early spring to spawn, remaining more active in cold water than most salmonids. They hold in deep pools and move into riffles during low-light periods.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the Smith River or Redwood Creek corridors in Redwood NP during winter rain events that raise and slightly color the water; look for fish holding behind large boulders or in tailouts of pools at first light.

animals.name: Lake Sturgeon
animals.behavior_notes: Lake Sturgeon spawn in fast-moving, rocky rivers in spring when water temperatures reach 55–65°F, and large individuals can be seen rolling at the surface or thrashing in shallow rapids. Outside of spawning, they are largely bottom-dwellers and very difficult to observe.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the Sturgeon River or Black River in Michigan's Upper Peninsula in late April; stand on bridges over rocky rapids and watch for large dark forms moving in the current — individuals can exceed 6 feet in length.

animals.name: White Sturgeon
parks: Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area
animals.behavior_notes: White Sturgeon are the largest freshwater fish in North America and can occasionally be seen rolling or jumping completely out of the water, a behavior whose purpose is still debated by scientists. Spring congregations in the Columbia and Snake rivers offer the best viewing opportunities.
animals.viewing_tips: Take a boat tour on the Columbia River near Bonneville Dam in April or May; fish congregate below the dam during spring flows and can be seen rolling near the surface or observed from dam viewing windows during fish counts.

animals.name: Paddlefish
animals.behavior_notes: Paddlefish congregate in large numbers below dams and in deep river pools during spring spawning runs, when they can be seen rolling at the surface and their distinctive paddle-shaped rostrum is occasionally visible. They filter-feed on zooplankton and are completely harmless.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the confluence of the Osage and Missouri rivers or below Keystone Lake in Oklahoma in March; look for large fish rolling near the surface at dawn — their enormous paddle is unmistakable if visible above the waterline.

animals.name: Alligator Gar
animals.behavior_notes: Alligator Gar are one of North America's largest freshwater fish and can be seen basking just below the surface or rolling to gulp air in warm, slow-moving water during summer. They are most active at dawn and dusk and often congregate in backwater bayous and oxbow lakes.
animals.viewing_tips: Canoe or kayak the slow bayous and sloughs of Big Thicket National Preserve in Texas at first light in June and July; scan the shaded margins of the water for the long, dark torpedo shape of a gar lying motionless just below the surface.

animals.name: Manta Ray
animals.behavior_notes: Oceanic Manta Rays frequent warm offshore waters and are often seen gracefully breaching completely out of the water, a spectacular behavior thought to be related to communication or parasite removal. They feed on plankton-rich surface waters and can gather in groups during plankton blooms.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a snorkel or dive trip from Biscayne NP or take a boat out to reef areas in summer; scan the surface for wingtips breaking the water and approach slowly — mantas are curious animals and may approach snorkelers on their own.

animals.name: Whale Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Whale sharks appear in warm Gulf and Atlantic waters during summer months, often feeding near the surface on fish spawn and plankton. They are slow-moving filter feeders and tend to linger near aggregations of baitfish.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a snorkel or dive charter out of Key West or Marathon that specifically targets whale shark sightings. Sightings are opportunistic and not guaranteed; joining a citizen science aggregation trip improves your odds.

animals.name: Hammerhead Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Scalloped and great hammerhead sharks frequent the warm shallow waters off southern Florida in late spring and summer, often hunting stingrays and schooling fish near grass flats and reef edges. They are more active at dawn and dusk when prey is on the move.
animals.viewing_tips: Dive or snorkel the reefs and grass flats of Biscayne National Park with a licensed charter; hammerheads are occasionally spotted from boats near channel edges. Stay calm and keep movements slow if one approaches.

animals.name: Great White Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great white sharks congregate near the Farallon Islands and the greater Point Reyes area in fall, drawn by the large elephant seal and harbor seal populations that haul out there. Breaching and surface predation events are most frequently observed during midday hours.
animals.viewing_tips: Join a shark-watching boat tour departing from San Francisco or Bodega Bay toward the Farallon Islands, which lie within the Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary. The NPS itself does not run shark tours but the adjacent marine sanctuary is the prime hotspot.

animals.name: Bull Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Bull sharks are uniquely adapted to tolerate freshwater and are known to travel deep into the rivers and estuaries of the Everglades during warm months. They are aggressive opportunistic feeders most active around dawn and dusk.
animals.viewing_tips: Take an airboat or ranger-led boat tour through Florida Bay and the mangrove estuaries of Everglades National Park. Bull sharks are rarely seen at the surface but are occasionally spotted in channels; do not swim in murky estuary waters.

animals.name: Coelacanth
parks: N/A — No US National Park habitat
animals.behavior_notes: The coelacanth is a critically rare deep-sea fish found only in the Indian Ocean and parts of the western Pacific, with no wild populations in US waters. It was long thought extinct before its rediscovery in 1938.
animals.viewing_tips: Coelacanths cannot be viewed in the wild in the United States. Your best opportunity is to see preserved specimens or exhibits at major natural history museums such as the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C.

animals.name: Brook Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Brook trout in Shenandoah's cold mountain streams are most active in spring and fall when water temperatures stay in their preferred 50–65°F range. During these periods they feed actively near riffles and pool edges in early morning light.
animals.viewing_tips: Walk the trail along any of Shenandoah's native brook trout streams such as Whiteoak Canyon Run or Jeremy's Run and look into clear pools from stream banks without casting a shadow on the water. A valid Virginia fishing license is required to fish; viewing only requires none.

animals.name: Largemouth Bass
animals.behavior_notes: Largemouth bass move into shallow coves and rocky shorelines at Lake Mead in spring to spawn, making them highly visible and accessible from shore or slow-moving watercraft. Males actively guard nests in water as shallow as 1–4 feet and can be observed directly.
animals.viewing_tips: Rent a kayak or canoe from Boulder Beach and paddle quietly into sheltered coves during early morning hours in April and May. Polarized sunglasses dramatically improve your ability to spot bass on spawning beds through the clear water.

animals.name: Monarch Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: Monarchs gather in large roosts during fall migration, often clustering on milkweed and goldenrod. Peak concentrations occur along coastal and inland flyways as they move toward Mexican overwintering grounds.
animals.viewing_tips: Look for clusters of orange wings on goldenrod and late-blooming wildflowers near coastal areas. Cape May, NJ and Peninsula Point, MI are famous concentration hotspots in September and October.

animals.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are active nectar feeders visiting a wide variety of flowering plants and frequently puddle on moist soil for minerals. Males are especially visible patrolling along woodland edges and forest clearings.
animals.viewing_tips: Focus on woodland edges, stream corridors, and flowering gardens with joe-pye weed, phlox, or butterfly bush. Calm, sunny mornings between 9 AM and noon are ideal when they are most actively foraging.

animals.name: Painted Lady Butterfly
parks: Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve
animals.behavior_notes: Painted Ladies are one of the most widely distributed butterflies in the world and undertake mass migrations in boom years. They strongly prefer open, sunny habitats and are vigorous nectar feeders on thistles, asters, and coneflowers.
animals.viewing_tips: Thistle patches in open meadows and roadsides are prime spots. In migration years, watch for large pulses passing through on warm, southerly winds; check butterfly count websites for real-time abundance reports.

animals.name: Luna Moth
animals.behavior_notes: Luna Moths are nocturnal and only live as adults for about one week, during which they do not eat and focus entirely on mating. They are strongly attracted to artificial lights on warm, humid nights near deciduous forests.
animals.viewing_tips: Check porch lights and mercury vapor light traps on warm nights above 55°F near hardwood forests with sweetgum, hickory, or walnut. Turn lights on after 9 PM and check wooden surfaces and screens for resting adults.

animals.name: Cecropia Moth
animals.behavior_notes: Cecropia Moths, North America's largest native moth, fly only at night and are most active in the hours just after midnight seeking mates. Like other giant silk moths, adults do not feed and live only one to two weeks.
animals.viewing_tips: Set up a white sheet with a UV blacklight in a wooded suburban or rural area on warm, calm nights with temperatures above 60°F. Check the sheet repeatedly between 10 PM and 2 AM for the best chance of spotting one.

animals.name: American Bumble Bee
animals.behavior_notes: American Bumble Bees forage actively on a wide variety of native wildflowers including clovers, sunflowers, and prairie blooms. Populations have declined sharply since the 1990s, making sightings increasingly uncommon across much of the former range.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit native prairie remnants and wildflower-rich habitats; focus on patches of monarda, sunflower, and clover. Document any sightings with iNaturalist photos as this species is now a candidate for federal endangered listing.

animals.name: Firefly (Eastern)
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Fireflies (Photinus pyralis) flash in a distinctive J-shaped pattern at dusk to attract mates, with peak activity occurring in the 30–45 minutes after sunset on warm, humid evenings. Synchronous firefly displays in the Smokies are a celebrated natural phenomenon drawing thousands of visitors.
animals.viewing_tips: Find an open meadow or forest edge away from artificial lights at least 30 minutes after sunset on a warm, calm night. Elkmont Campground in Great Smoky Mountains NP hosts a famous synchronous display in late May to mid-June requiring advance lottery reservations.

animals.name: Periodical Cicada
animals.behavior_notes: Periodical Cicadas emerge en masse when soil temperatures reach 64°F, with billions appearing simultaneously in 13- or 17-year cycles. Males chorus loudly in treetops during midday to attract females, creating one of nature's most spectacular acoustic events.
animals.viewing_tips: Track active broods using the Cicada Safari app to find emergence hotspots in your region. Visit deciduous forest edges in suburban and rural areas and look for emerging nymphs climbing tree trunks in the evening before a major emergence day.

animals.name: Dragonfly (Common Green Darner)
parks: Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge
animals.behavior_notes: Common Green Darners undertake a remarkable multi-generational migration along the Atlantic Coast and other flyways, moving south in large swarms on northwest winds following cold fronts in fall. They hunt actively over open water and marshes, hawking smaller insects in flight.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal wetlands and shorelines the day after a cold front passes in late August through October and scan low over water and reedy margins. Cape May Point, NJ is the premier dragonfly migration watchsite in North America.

animals.name: Praying Mantis
animals.behavior_notes: Praying Mantises reach adult size by late summer and are at peak abundance and visibility in August through October when females are large and heavily gravid. They are sit-and-wait ambush predators that remain motionless in vegetation for extended periods waiting for prey.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan goldenrod, tall grasses, and garden flower heads slowly and carefully, as mantises rely on camouflage and are easily overlooked. Searching in the early morning when dew makes vegetation heavy and mantises slow is the most productive strategy.

animals.name: Walking Stick
animals.behavior_notes: Walking sticks are most active at dusk and night during summer months when they feed on leaves of oak, cherry, and other deciduous trees. They rely heavily on camouflage and remain motionless during the day, making evening searches far more productive.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan the undersides of oak and cherry leaves slowly with a red-light flashlight after dark. Look for movement rather than the insect itself, as their camouflage is extraordinarily effective against foliage.

animals.name: Tarantula (Desert Blonde)
animals.behavior_notes: Male desert blonde tarantulas emerge from their burrows in late summer and fall to actively roam in search of females during mating season, making them far more visible than at any other time of year. Females remain near their burrows but may be spotted at the entrance during warm evenings.
animals.viewing_tips: Drive slowly along desert roads near Saguaro National Park at dusk and early evening during September and October when males are actively roaming. Walking desert trails at twilight with a flashlight also increases sighting chances significantly.

animals.name: Black Widow Spider
animals.behavior_notes: Black widows are most active during warm months, emerging at night to tend their irregular, messy webs built low to the ground in sheltered, dark spaces such as rock crevices, woodpiles, and dense brush. They are rarely aggressive but will defend their webs if disturbed.
animals.viewing_tips: Search with a UV flashlight after dark — black widow silk fluoresces under ultraviolet light, making webs and spiders much easier to locate in rocky desert terrain. Check under rocks, logs, and in crevices carefully and never reach into unseen spaces.

animals.name: American Horseshoe Crab
animals.behavior_notes: American horseshoe crabs mass on mid-Atlantic beaches during high tides around new and full moons in May and June to spawn, with females laying eggs in the sand while smaller males cluster around them. This ancient spawning ritual is one of the most spectacular wildlife events on the East Coast.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit Delaware or New Jersey beaches during high tide on nights surrounding the full or new moon in late May for the peak spawning event. Walk the shoreline quietly with a dim red flashlight and watch for the domed shells rolling in with the waves.

animals.name: Giant Water Bug
animals.behavior_notes: Giant water bugs are ambush predators lurking in shallow freshwater ponds, marshes, and slow streams, where they prey on tadpoles, small fish, and even frogs during the warmer months. They are also nocturnal fliers attracted to lights near water, especially during warm spring and summer evenings.
animals.viewing_tips: Shine a bright flashlight into the shallows of still freshwater ponds and marshy edges at night and watch for large, oval brown insects clinging to vegetation or swimming aggressively just below the surface. Lights near water in warm months will also attract flying individuals.

animals.name: Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific octopuses emerge from rocky dens during cooler months to hunt crabs and mollusks along the intertidal zone. They are most active at low tide near dawn and dusk when hunting pressure from larger predators decreases.
animals.viewing_tips: Look in rocky tide pools and under ledges during low tide events; bring a flashlight and move slowly to avoid startling them into jetting away.

animals.name: Giant Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Giant Pacific Octopuses are most visible in late winter and early spring when males venture from deep dens to find mates in shallow subtidal zones. Females guard egg clutches in dens from winter into spring, making them detectable by careful observers.
animals.viewing_tips: Join a guided scuba or snorkel tour from Port Angeles or Puget Sound — shore-based sightings are rare but possible at very low tides near large rocky overhangs.

animals.name: Bioluminescent Dinoflagellates
animals.behavior_notes: Bioluminescent dinoflagellates bloom in warm, nutrient-rich waters during summer months, emitting blue-green light when disturbed by waves or movement. Blooms are most intense on moonless nights following calm, warm weather.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit on a new moon night and allow 20 minutes for your eyes to dark-adapt; kayaking through the water or wading in shallow bays will trigger the glowing effect most dramatically.

animals.name: Jellyfish (Moon)
animals.behavior_notes: Moon jellyfish aggregate in large surface blooms during summer months, drifting with currents in bays and harbors. They feed on plankton and are often visible from docks, kayaks, and calm shorelines.
animals.viewing_tips: Walk along pier edges or paddle in a kayak through calm coves during summer — blooms can number in the thousands and are easily spotted just beneath the water surface.

animals.name: Dungeness Crab
animals.behavior_notes: Dungeness crabs migrate into shallower estuaries and bays in fall and early winter to molt and mate, making them more accessible to shore-based observers. Males become especially active at low tide as they search rocky and sandy flats.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit tide pools and estuaries at low tide in the early morning; look under rocks and along sandy mudflat edges where crabs forage for clams and worms.

animals.name: American Lobster
animals.behavior_notes: American lobsters move into shallower nearshore waters during summer when water temperatures warm, making them more observable in rocky subtidal zones. They emerge from crevices at dawn and dusk to forage for mussels, urchins, and fish.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling along rocky underwater ledges in Acadia's coastal waters at dawn offers the best chance of a sighting; alternatively, visit working lobster wharves where trap hauls are brought in each morning.

animals.name: Coral (Elkhorn)
animals.behavior_notes: Elkhorn coral spawns once a year shortly after the full moon in summer, releasing bundles of eggs and sperm in a spectacular nighttime event. During daylight hours, the branching structures provide shelter for hundreds of reef fish species.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a snorkel or dive trip through Biscayne National Park's authorized concessionaires — Elkhorn coral is federally protected and critically endangered, so maintain a safe distance and never touch the coral.

animals.name: Coral (Brain)
animals.behavior_notes: Brain corals are slow-growing, long-lived reef builders that remain most visible and vibrant during spring when water clarity is at its peak before summer storm season. They extend their polyps to feed on zooplankton primarily at night but are easily observable year-round.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel the Trunk Bay Underwater Trail in Virgin Islands NP for well-marked brain coral formations; midday sun angles provide the best light penetration for photography and viewing.

animals.name: Sea Anemone
animals.behavior_notes: Sea anemones are sessile filter feeders that extend their colorful tentacles fully during incoming tides in spring when plankton blooms peak. At low tide they retract into compact blobs on rocks, but during high and mid tide they are brilliantly open and active.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit tide pools at mid to incoming tide rather than low tide — anemones are far more visible and photogenic when their tentacles are extended; look in shaded, water-filled pools for giant green anemones.

animals.name: Starfish (Sunflower Sea Star)
animals.behavior_notes: The Sunflower Sea Star is critically endangered due to Sea Star Wasting Disease and population crashes since 2013, but occasional individuals can still be spotted in colder northern waters during winter months. They are active predators that move surprisingly fast across rocky substrates hunting urchins and clams.
animals.viewing_tips: Sightings are extremely rare and should be reported to iNaturalist or NOAA — if you spot one, document it with photos without touching it, as the species is critically endangered and populations remain severely depleted.

animals.name: Pacific Sea Nettle
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific Sea Nettles drift with ocean currents during summer months, often forming large aggregations near the surface. Their long trailing tentacles and orange-tinted bells are most visible in calm, clear nearshore waters.
animals.viewing_tips: Look for their distinctive golden-brown bells from kayaks, glass-bottom boats, or snorkeling near kelp forest edges around Channel Islands. Calm days with minimal chop offer the best visibility; avoid touching as tentacles can sting.

animals.name: Mantis Shrimp
animals.behavior_notes: Mantis shrimp are most active at dawn and dusk when they emerge from burrows in coral rubble and sandy seafloor to hunt. Spring warming of water temperatures increases their foraging activity and makes sightings more likely.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or dive over seagrass beds and coral rubble areas in Biscayne's shallow lagoon, scanning burrow entrances carefully at low light hours. A dive light is helpful for spotting their iridescent coloring tucked just inside crevices.
